# Shopware Storefront — what breaks when you override a block

A JavaScript plugin reaches into the markup by selector. Replace the markup without the selector and the plugin still initialises, finds nothing, and silently does nothing — no console error, no failed request, just a button that stopped working.

**120 templates carry at least one selector a plugin queries: 160 distinct selectors across 62 plugins, 413 template-block-selector pairs. A further 204 places hand options from Twig into a plugin.**

## Contents

- [How to use this](#how-to-use-this)
- [The rules](#the-rules)

- [By selector](#by-selector)
- [Selectors the analytics events read](#selectors-the-analytics-events-read)

## How to use this

Before overriding a block, look the template up below. Every selector listed under the block you are replacing must still exist in your markup — on the same element, in the same nesting relationship to its plugin's root element.

A selector is listed against the **innermost block** containing it. Overriding a parent block replaces its children too, so a parent inherits every requirement below it.

## The rules

- **`js-` prefixed classes are contracts, not styling.** They exist only so JavaScript can find the element. Never rename one, and never style against one.
- **`data-*` attributes bind the plugin itself.** Losing the attribute means the plugin never initialises on that element at all.
- **Nesting matters.** Most plugins query inside `this.el`, so a child selector must stay a descendant of the element carrying the plugin's own attribute.
- **Keep `{{ parent() }}`** where you only add markup — it is the cheapest way to keep every selector you did not think about.
- **Test the behaviour, not the layout.** These failures are invisible in a screenshot: click the button, submit the form, change the quantity.

## Values handed from Twig into a plugin

A plugin reads its options from `data-<dash-case-name>-options` (and `-config`) on its own element, JSON-encoded. These are the values the template computes and the plugin depends on: remove the attribute, move it to another element, or drop the variable that feeds it, and the plugin falls back to its `static options` defaults — usually wrong, always silent.

**When overriding a block that carries one of these, keep the attribute on the same element and keep whatever `{% set %}` produced its value.** If the value comes from the page struct, it only exists on pages that provide it.

## Selectors the analytics events read

The Google Analytics events read the rendered markup directly to build their payload. Losing one of these breaks tracking without breaking the page — the most expensive kind of silent failure, because it is noticed weeks later in a report.
